newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean president in talks to defuse labour crisis.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean president in talks to defuse labour crisis.

text.p: South Korean President Kim Young-sam met opposition leaders on Tuesday to try to forge a compromise over a controversial labour law that ignited more than three weeks of wildcat strikes.

Kim was holding talks with Kim Dae-jung of the main opposition National Congress for New Politics and Kim Jong-pil of the United Liberal Democratic Party, a presidential aide said. Lee Hong-koo, chairman of the ruling New Korea Party, also attended.
The aide said no time limit was set for the talks that began around midday (0300 GMT) at the presidential Blue House. Yonhap Television News said the meeting would last about two hours.

Attention has been riveted on the meeting since President Kim, in a dramatic turnaround, agreed on Monday to discuss opposition criticism of the law, which was rammed through parliament on December 26.

The legislation allows firms to sack workers and replace strikers in a bid to free up the labour market, thus cutting corporate costs and improving competitiveness. The law also bans the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions until 2000.
Unionists returned to work on Monday after the confederation called off indefinite strikes and agreed to limit industrial action to once a week on Wednesdays.

A spokesman for the National Congress said the opposition parties would seek to reopen debate on the law, have arrest warrants for fugitive unionists withdrawn and demand an apology from President Kim for the way the law was passed.
The president had previously rejected repeated demands by opposition parties to discuss the new bill.
Political analysts said Kim might agree to supplement the labour law with more guarantees of job security and advance the timetable for recognising the outlawed confederation.
Newspaper reports said the ruling party may be prepared to reopen debate on the law in the National Assembly.
Confederation leader Kwon Young-kil, who is sheltering from arrest at Seoul's Myongdong Cathedral, urged the government to scrap the law and drop legal action against union leaders.

"If not, and if the government tries to whitewash the situation, we will not only go ahead with the Wednesday general strike but escalate protests in the future by rearranging the timetable for an all-out strike struggle," he told reporters.
In a sign authorities want a peaceful end to violent confrontation with labour unions, prosecutors have said they would hold off arresting Kwon and six deputies at the church.

The officially-sanctioned Federation of Korean Trade Unions issued a statement urging the government to delay implementation of the legislation until June to give all parties time to review the law, which is due to take effect on March 1.
While many agree South Korea's rigid labour practices need overhauling, there is anger at the way the law was adopted.
Businessmen warned that a political compromise risked papering over their core concerns.

An official at the Korean Employers' Association said he believed the government would have to yield to pressure to immediately legalise the confederation, which had led the strikes that hobbled key export industries.
"But deals should not be sought to make it more difficult for companies to lay off workers. This will worsen the labour market's rigidity," he said.
Political analysts said Kim would seek a compromise in a way to avoid becoming a lame duck in his last year of office.

"If he declares the law void and agrees to start anew, that will be a full surrender and he would lose control over the national agenda for the rest of his tenure," said Kim Young-jin, a labour expert at Korea University.
President Kim, due to end his five-year term early next year, is barred by the constitution from seeking re-election but is expected to try to install a protege.

Stocks fell by midday as fears of a correction after Monday's rally sparked selling orders and investors turned skittish, fearing the talks would not lead to a resolution of the labour unrest, brokers said.
The main stock index dropped 8.39 points or 1.17 percent to 710.07 by the morning close.
